title: Scrunch vs Ahrefs: AI visibility tracking comparison
content:
Scrunch and Ahrefs Brand Radar both track brand visibility in AI answers, but they solve different problems. Scrunch is purpose-built for AEO: it monitors AI citations, audits AI crawlability, and actively optimizes how AI bots experience your site. Ahrefs Brand Radar is an add-on to the broader Ahrefs SEO platform, built for teams that want AI visibility alongside traditional search data, backlinks, and web mentions in one place.
If you haven’t benchmarked your AI visibility yet, start with HubSpot’s free AEO Grader — a scored snapshot of how ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini represent your brand today, no account required.
Scrunch and Ahrefs Brand Radar are not the same type of product. Understanding what each one actually tracks is the most important step before evaluating pricing, coverage, or ROI.
Scrunch is a purpose-built AI visibility platform. It tracks brand share of voice across AI answers, sentiment in AI-generated responses, and which domains and pages are most frequently cited. Beyond brand monitoring, it tracks AI search trends for prompt volumes and product-level shopping visibility to show how brands rank in AI-driven purchase recommendations.
Ahrefs Brand Radar is an add-on module within the broader Ahrefs platform. It tracks brand presence across AI answers and layers that data alongside traditional search demand, web mentions, video, and Reddit. Where Scrunch is purpose-built for AI visibility, Brand Radar is designed for teams that want AI monitoring without leaving the Ahrefs ecosystem.
AI visibility data is only as trustworthy as the methodology behind it. This is where I’d encourage any team to push harder before they buy.
Scrunch uses a combination of browser automation and official platform APIs, then applies machine learning and NLP to surface brand mentions, sentiment, and citation patterns. Prompts run daily for the first 14 days after setup, then shift to a 72-hour refresh cadence by default. You can manually trigger a fresh response at any time.
One nuance worth noting: Scrunch’s prompt architecture converts keyword data into prompts rather than sampling actual user queries from live AI traffic. For teams tracking a specific set of brand-relevant questions, this gives you precise control. For teams trying to model what real buyers are actually asking, it’s a gap worth acknowledging.
Ahrefs Brand Radar draws from a pool of 406M+ total monthly prompts derived from real user keywords (not synthetic) and lets you build custom queries to filter by prompt type, brand, and AI platform. The scale is an advantage: you’re benchmarking against a broader signal, not just the prompts your team wrote.
The documented limitations are worth flagging: third-party reviews report accuracy gaps in ChatGPT and Perplexity tracking specifically. Claude is not currently covered, which matters for teams whose buyers use Claude for professional research. Grok is included.
When setting up Scrunch, start by validating which AI models are actually visiting your site and what content they consume. Scrunch’s Agent Traffic tool tracks visits from bots like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity, helping you distinguish useful AI traffic from noise.
From there, use Scrunch’s Site Maps feature to see how AI agents interpret your site structure and identify which pages have blockers preventing AI systems from parsing them. The combination of Agent Traffic and Site Maps gives you a ground-level picture of AI crawlability before you start optimizing anything.
Two questions that matter before any platform purchase:
Pro tip: AI visibility reporting should track directional trends rather than single-point metrics alone. A single citation count at one moment in time is nearly meaningless; AI response variability is too high. Ask each vendor to show you trend lines, not snapshots.
My experience has taught me that the wrong tool isn’t usually the most expensive one. It’s the one that tracks the wrong thing for your goals.
Best for: AEO-focused marketing teams and enterprise brands with dedicated AI visibility programs.
Best for: SEO-led teams that want a unified view of AI visibility, traditional search, and web mentions.
Searchers comparing Scrunch vs Ahrefs typically want to know what each tool tracks and how it collects data. The more useful question is: what problem are you actually trying to solve on day one?
If your primary question is “why doesn’t my brand appear in AI answers for buying-stage prompts, and what do I fix?” Scrunch’s workflow is built around that question.
If your primary question is “how is our brand performing across all discovery channels including AI, search, Reddit, and YouTube?” Ahrefs Brand Radar gives you a single dashboard for that view.
If you’re not sure yet and want a low-risk way to benchmark before buying either, HubSpot AEO starts at $50/month with actionable recommendations, citation analysis, and a competitive visibility score. AEO Grader supports low-risk benchmarking for teams not ready to buy a platform.
Searchers comparing Scrunch vs Ahrefs compare pricing, AI engine coverage, and data retention. Here’s the honest breakdown for 2026.
Scrunch’s Brand Core plan starts at $250/month and includes 125 unique tracked prompts, 5 site audits per month, 1 brand workspace, 5 user licenses, and coverage across 4 LLMs: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AIO, and Copilot. A 7-day free trial is available with no credit card required.
The Agency Core plan runs $500/month and includes 250 prompts, 5 audits per brand, 3 brand workspaces, 3 pitch workspaces, and unlimited user licenses. Agency Enterprise is available for custom scaling. Brand Enterprise (custom pricing) unlocks AXP, custom prompts, custom audits, API/SSO, and expands to 9 LLMs (adding Claude, Gemini, Meta AI, Grok, and Google AI Mode). Note: AXP is Enterprise-only.
Ahrefs Brand Radar is available as a standalone product or bundled with Ahrefs SEO plans. Standalone pricing starts at $199/month (entry), $398/month for Select Platforms, or $699/month for All Platforms (full 406M+ prompt database, 2,500 custom checks, includes Grok).
For AEO-only teams, the $199/month standalone entry point is the lowest-friction way in. Bundled in Ahrefs SEO plans starting at $129/month (Lite). Custom Prompts only: Basic $50/mo (2,500 checks) to Scale $250/mo (25,000 checks).
On day one with Scrunch’s Brand Core plan, you get coverage across 4 LLMs: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AIO, and Copilot, with 125 custom prompts, 5 site audits, and 5 user licenses. That’s a viable starting set for most B2B brands. Note: Claude coverage requires a Brand Enterprise upgrade.
Pro tip: Website Grader helps assess technical site health before platform onboarding. Weak technical foundations limit what AI visibility tools can find and report, so run a site health check before you start tracking.
The table below compares tracking focus, data sources, AI engine coverage, pricing, retention, and best-fit teams across Scrunch, Ahrefs Brand Radar, and HubSpot AEO.
Getting to first value is faster with one tool than the other, and it depends on where your team currently operates.
Onboarding involves building your prompt library (which prompts to track, which personas, which competitors) and running Scrunch’s Site Maps to understand how AI agents currently see your site. Core plans include Google Single Sign-On. Enterprise plans add SAML or OIDC SSO, Looker Studio integration, Query API access, and advanced API access so you can pull Scrunch data into existing dashboards.
Scrunch’s AXP (Enterprise-only) is implemented at the edge, meaning it integrates into your site’s content delivery layer and serves AI-optimized pages to bots without touching your human-facing CMS or website workflow. It reduces token loads by up to 26% to unblock AI agents stuck on complex website markup. The two experiences (human site and AI-optimized site) run in parallel.
Brand Radar activates as a module within your existing Ahrefs account or as a standalone product. No separate installation or new vendor relationship is required for existing Ahrefs users, which is the main implementation advantage. You set up brand monitoring by defining the prompts and brands you want tracked, then Brand Radar pulls from its 406M+ total monthly prompt pool to surface your visibility data. The MCP Server lets you pull live Ahrefs data directly into Claude or ChatGPT for in-workflow analysis. Bot Analytics is available for tracking AI bot behavior on your site, and IndexNow integration is included.
The limitation here is the same as the product limitation: Brand Radar inherits the Ahrefs platform roadmap. If your AI visibility use case grows faster than the Ahrefs product team prioritizes it, you won’t have an escalation path outside of switching tools.
Every AI visibility tool has limitations in 2026, and I think it’s worth being direct about them.
Scrunch’s AXP (Enterprise-only) actively delivers two separate experiences: a token-light, AI-optimized version of your site to bots — reducing token loads by up to 26% to unblock AI agents stuck on complex markup — and your traditional website to human visitors. Your team needs to evaluate whether maintaining this dual-delivery architecture fits your technical strategy and risk tolerance before committing.
My view: AEO complements SEO rather than replacing it. Scrunch itself acknowledges this: the traditional human-facing site remains intact for SEO, while the optimized edge experience handles AEO. Brands that neglect the SEO foundation while chasing AI visibility tend to end up with neither.
Yes, and it’s a legitimate strategy for larger teams. The most sensible pairing: Ahrefs Brand Radar for SEO teams monitoring AI share of voice alongside traditional search performance, and Scrunch or HubSpot AEO for the content team running AEO sprints against specific prompt sets. There’s coverage overlap on ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, so budget for some redundancy if you go this route.
Data methodology determines how trustworthy and actionable visibility reporting feels, which is why having two methodologically different tools tracking the same engines can actually improve your confidence in the data.
Visibility data is only worth what you do with it. This is where most teams stall. They have a score, a share of voice number, a list of prompts where they’re not showing up, but no systematic way to turn that into content that actually gets cited.
The workflow I’ve found most effective: start with the prompts where you’re losing to competitors. Look at what sources the AI is citing when it answers those prompts. Those sources (specific pages, publications, review platforms, forums) become your content targeting list. You’re not trying to rank; you’re trying to become a trusted source for the sources that AI trusts.
Pro tip : Download the State of AEO report . HubSpot saw a 433% improvement in brand citations, with data from 4,000+ global marketers on best practices, top citation themes across 6+ answer engines, and B2B vs. B2C comparisons.
Scrunch’s Insights feature is the bridge between data and content work. Rather than just flagging low visibility, Insights pairs each diagnosis with a specific recommended action. For example, it might identify that a competitor is appearing in AI answers for a category you should own, then recommend creating content that highlights a specific feature to differentiate your brand in AI responses.
This diagnosis-plus-recommendation structure is what separates Scrunch from tools that only report visibility scores. You end up with a prioritized content brief, not just a dashboard number to stare at.
For pipeline attribution, Scrunch’s Agent Traffic and Shopping features connect visibility to site behavior: Agent Traffic tells you which AI bots are consuming your site and what, while Shopping tracks which products are winning AI-driven commerce recommendations. Together they give you a clearer line from content investment to commercial outcome.
The Scrunch vs Ahrefs comparison doesn’t exist in isolation. It’s worth understanding where each sits relative to the broader SEO platform category.
Semrush frames modern discovery as a “combined SEO + AI discovery problem” and advocates for dominating both Google and AI search simultaneously. Its SEO Toolkit analyzes a database of 26.8 billion keywords and tracks up to 5,000 keywords daily on its Advanced plan, with keyword cannibalization tracking available on Pro and above. Semrush also offers a 7-day free trial across its SEO, AI Visibility, and Social toolkits.
Keyword difficulty scores are not interchangeable across platforms. Different tools weight different signals, so a score of 40 in one tool rarely means the same thing as 40 in another. Always benchmark KD scores within a single platform rather than across tools.
For AI visibility specifically, “keyword difficulty” doesn’t translate cleanly. The right equivalent is prompt competitiveness: how many credible, well-cited sources appear when an AI model answers a specific prompt, and how hard is it to become one of them? Scrunch’s AI Search Trends feature approaches this by tracking which topics are actively gaining or losing momentum in AI prompts, giving you a directional read on where competition is intensifying.
Yes. The most practical pairing is Ahrefs Brand Radar for SEO teams monitoring AI visibility alongside traditional search, and Scrunch or HubSpot AEO for content teams running active AEO programs. There’s meaningful coverage overlap on ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, so budget for some redundancy if you go this route.
HubSpot’s free AEO Grader gives you a one-time scored snapshot across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini with no account required. AEO Sensor gives you ongoing industry-level AI visibility and citation trends, also free. Between the two, you can establish meaningful benchmarks before buying any paid platform.
In Scrunch, there are two concrete ROI signals. First, Agent Traffic: this shows which AI bots are actually consuming your site, giving you proof that AI systems are engaging with your content rather than ignoring it. Second, the Shopping feature tracks which specific products win shelf space in AI-driven commerce prompts, so you can tie visibility changes to purchase-intent outcomes.
Semrush is building toward combining AI visibility scores with traditional SEO metrics, traffic data, and Google Analytics conversions in a single ROI view, though this is positioned as a future capability.
Pro tip : Avoid using raw citation count as a primary KPI. It rewards volume over quality, and a citation in a vague AI answer to a low-intent prompt is worth less than no appearance at all.
No. Both Scrunch and Semrush are explicit on this. Semrush frames it as a “combined SEO + AI discovery problem” and positions the goal as dominating both Google and AI search simultaneously. Scrunch’s own architecture makes the same point structurally: its AXP serves an optimized experience to AI bots while the traditional human-facing site remains intact for SEO. The two channels are managed in parallel, not as replacements for each other.
Neither Scrunch nor Semrush prescribes a universal refresh timeline, but both emphasize continuous monitoring over periodic audits. Scrunch’s AI Search Trends tool tracks which AI topics are actively gaining or losing momentum, so you’re updating content as actual demand shifts rather than on an arbitrary schedule.
Semrush provides daily data updates for its tracked AI prompts and AI rankings, and its SEO Content Toolkit is designed specifically for continuously refreshing, rephrasing, and optimizing content for AI systems.
The practical rule: monitor your highest-priority prompts continuously, and refresh content when you see a sustained drop in citations or sentiment on those specific prompts. A data-triggered refresh will always outperform a calendar-triggered one.

title: Google Went ‘Not Provided’ In 2011 And Blinded Us, ChatGPT Just Shipped Its Version via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester
content:
The attribution you are waiting for from ChatGPT is coming, and it is not coming to you. I ran a survey this month ( it’s still open; please take it ) asking whether dedicated AI visibility platforms are worth paying for, and I deliberately never asked about attribution. It showed up anyway. One consultant wrote that the whole problem is tying visibility, citations, and mentions to dollars. An agency owner managing over a dozen clients answered the “what’s your biggest-unanswered-question” prompt with a single word and an exclamation point: attribution! Another respondent put it more wearily: that tracking is only the first step, so what comes next.
Two different frustrations hide inside that one word, attribution. One is whether a tracker reads your AI visibility accurately at all. The other is whether that visibility can be tied to revenue. This piece is about the second. The first runs underneath it, and I come back to it at the end.
That corner has stayed dark for a reason, and it is not the reason most people think. The instinct is to treat missing attribution as a gap some vendor will eventually fill, the way rank tracking filled in twenty years ago. It will not fill in that way. The click-path attribution that organic search practitioners were trained to expect, the deterministic line from impression to session to conversion, is gone, and AI did not kill it. Referral traffic from AI answers is real but tiny, under one percent of total traffic on most sites, which means the thing people are asking for was never going to be answered by watching their own analytics. So let me toss a flashlight at the corner. Here is where attribution stands, why it stands there, and an idea about what you do starting tomorrow.
Third-party cookies went into slow deprecation, Apple’s App Tracking Transparency cut off a huge slice of mobile signal, Google Analytics moved to modeled conversions rather than counted ones, and media mix modeling, a technique older than most of the people now using it, came roaring back precisely because the clean deterministic path had frayed. Every one of those shifts happened for its own reasons and none of them involved ChatGPT. LLMs did not break attribution. They arrived after the break and made it impossible to keep pretending. The measurement world you are standing in was already modeled, probabilistic, and permission-dependent before answer engines entered the picture, and that is the ground we are now building on.
Attribution from the platforms is coming, but it is arriving through the ads door, not the webmaster-tools door. The signal a paying advertiser needs and the signal a free organic practitioner wants are the same signal. A platform will build that signal for the person spending money and withhold it from the person who is not, because there is no business reason to give away for free what someone else will pay for.
We have watched this movie. In 2011, Google encrypted organic search referrals and organic keyword data vanished into the not-provided bucket, while paid search advertisers kept getting richer and richer conversion data. Same query intent, same underlying behavior, monetized on one side and starved on the other. Organic SEO spent a decade angry about it. (Maybe you still are?)
ChatGPT just shipped its version, and you can read both halves of it in OpenAI’s own documentation. On the organic side, the controls OpenAI gives webmasters are switches, not meters. You can allow OAI-SearchBot so you appear in ChatGPT’s answers, or disallow GPTBot so your content is not used in training. Toggles. On or off. What you cannot do is measure via OpenAI. On the paid side, OpenAI has already built a full server-to-server conversions pipeline : a pixel, an events API keyed to an Ads Manager account, standard events like order_created carrying amount, currency, and item-level detail, deduplication between browser and server, and a privacy-preserving identifier to tie exposure to outcome. That is closed-loop conversion attribution. It exists right now. It sits behind an ad account. The organic operator on the same platform gets a robots.txt file and best wishes.
Nobody at OpenAI needed to say Google’s name for this to happen. The not-provided lesson has been in plain sight for more than a decade, in every conference post-mortem and forum thread written since 2011, and the lesson is precise: taking access away costs you years of goodwill, so do not take it away; simply never grant it. Google paid for its mistake because it was a taking, and people fight takings . A designed absence generates no protest, only a low, unfocused unease. That knowledge was ambient. Any competent operator building an answer engine already had it.
Which is why this is not really an OpenAI story. Plot the model companies along a line by their stated reason to exist, a sell-to-serve spectrum if you want a handle for it, meaning where each one sits between built to sell and built to serve. OpenAI is running hard at commerce and ads, so it builds the paid measurement loop first and most visibly. Perplexity is chasing a slice of the discovery-and-shopping pie and moves in the same direction. Google already is an ad company. Anthropic frames itself around safety and long-term benefit and has the least structural reason to build an ads attribution layer at all. The doors differ, and the timing differs, but read the whole line and the conclusion holds in every seat: None of these companies has an incentive to hand free, item-level organic attribution to SEOs. The commercially driven ones gate it behind ad spend. The mission-driven ones simply have better things to build. Do not expect it from ChatGPT is the narrow version. The real version is do not expect it anywhere, sadly.
When practitioners say attribution, they are usually blending three different problems that have three different answers . The first is referral attribution , meaning did an AI answer link to you, did someone click, did that session convert. That one is measurable today, because the click carries a referrer into your own analytics. The second is incrementality , meaning not who clicked but whether your visibility caused lift you would not otherwise have gotten. The third is influence , the dark-funnel case, meaning the buyer read your brand inside an AI answer, never clicked, and showed up three weeks later through a branded search. Referral you can see now. Incrementality you can prove yourself. Influence is genuinely hard. The mistake is treating all three as one blocked pipe, when two of them are already flowing and need nothing from the platforms at all.
Start with referral classification , and do it properly, because the default is wrong. AI sessions do not reliably self-label, and referrer strings alone will misfile a large share of them into direct or organic. Tag deliberately with UTMs where you control the link, build a classification rule that combines referrer with landing-page and query patterns rather than trusting the referrer field on its own, and treat the number you get as a floor, because unattributable and cross-window purchases bias every honest count downward. That gets you an accurate read on the one layer that is visible.
Then run incrementality yourself, which is the layer most teams skip because it takes design rather than a dashboard. Hold out a set of geographies and change nothing in them while you push visibility work everywhere else, or run on-off tests over defined windows, or track a fixed set of queries before and after a content push and watch what moves. This is causal measurement, and it belongs to you, not to the platform, which means the opacity of the black box does not touch it.
For the dark funnel, borrow the muscle B2B has used for twenty years, because this is not new-hard; it is old-hard wearing a new coat. Self-reported attribution, the how-did-you-hear-about-us field at the point of conversion, catches influence that no pixel will ever see. Branded-demand correlation, watching whether branded search and direct navigation rise as your AI visibility rises, gives you a defensible read at the aggregate level. Brand-lift studies do the same with more rigor when the budget is there. None of it is deterministic, and that is fine, because deterministic is not on the menu for anyone anymore.
Ask what data source closes the loop, and listen carefully to the answer. If the honest answer is first-party, meaning their agents on your site, your Google Analytics 4, your CRM, then what they sell is real but bounded, and it lives at the referral layer. If the answer implies signal drawn from inside OpenAI or Anthropic, they are either misrepresenting a referrer-detection method or lying to you. There is no third source. That single question separates the credible from the theatrical faster than any feature list.
Attribution counts orders from sessions you classified as AI-referred. Some of those buyers would have found you anyway. Incrementality measures the lift you actually caused, and it requires the experiments described above. Report attribution as attribution, and reserve the word incremental for the cases where you ran the test. The vendors who keep that distinction clean read as trustworthy. The ones who collapse it and promise to prove ROI are the 2026 reissue of guaranteed-first-page SEO, and they will age exactly as well, I think.
The players with defensible revenue measurement all sidestep the black box and run on first-party data. Some vendors compute attribution by joining their own storefront sessions to checkout events against a sitewide baseline, and the numbers that get reported vary wildly, which is the honest headline. Microsoft Clarity’s study of 1,200 publisher sites found AI-referred visitors converting to sign-ups at eleven times the rate of organic search, while the peer-reviewed work in Marketing Science , 973 sites and 20 billion dollars in revenue, found organic LLM traffic converting below every traditional channel except paid social. I think both are true, and that is the point. The channel is small, high-intent, and wildly uneven, and it is not even measured the same way twice. Others resolve the loop the same first-party way, routing through affiliate infrastructure or handing purchase reporting back to your own analytics. The pattern under all of it is the tell: Everyone credible closes the loop with data you already own, because that is the only door open.
Referral classification standardizes and gets boring, as the engines increasingly identify themselves and the analytics tools catch up. Attribution proper gets monetized as an ads product, gated and paid, exactly along the line OpenAI has already drawn in its documentation. And the honest vendors converge on the attribution-versus-incrementality language, because the market eventually punishes the ones who oversold. None of that returns free organic attribution to you, because none of it ever had a reason to.
The attribution requests were loud, but they were the sharp, nameable tip of something larger and more corrosive. As I read the early open-text answers together, what surfaces is not mainly a demand for better numbers; it is a refusal to believe the numbers already on offer. Respondents said they do not trust the trackers, that they cannot tell whether any of it is accurate, that they are struggling to invest because they do not trust the results. That is not a feature gap. That is a trust deficit, and part of it is the correct read of a market built on designed absences and overselling. But I would be lying if I put all of it there. Some of that unease is old thinking meeting a new situation, practitioners carrying SEO reflexes into an environment that does not run on them and skipping the work of learning what actually changed, because “GEO = SEO” is a more comfortable story than the truth. I can’t tell you how big that share is and nobody can measure it cleanly; we read it off what we see and hear online, at conferences, etc. But if it is even a third of the industry’s working mindset, that is not something a vendor comes along and fixes. That is a literacy problem, and it belongs to all of us.
If you are wrestling with this in your own stack, tell me where your loop breaks, in the comments or directly, because the playbook here is still being written and the field’s real answers are coming from practitioners, not vendors. And if you want the longer argument for why the underlying systems, not the dashboards, are where this literacy has to live, that is the whole spine of The Machine Layer .
This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes .
